facts.fact: WHO states that DHIS2 reached 100% national geographic coverage by March 2023 but that consistent reporting from health facilities remains a challenge; it gives no count or share of facilities, or of primary facilities, entering reports.

WHO and the Ministry of Health made supervisory visits to five health facilities in Suq Aljuma municipality, Tripoli, on 16-23 December 2024, assessing the facilities' DHIS2 data entry compliance, reporting timeliness and completeness and local data management capacity.

WHO reports that the first round of DHIS2 supervisory visits, to five health facilities in Suq Aljuma on 16-23 December 2024, led to noticeable improvements in data quality and reporting compliance, with further visits planned for 2025 in eastern and southern Libya; four workshops in the western and central regions trained municipal Health Services Administration Officers and HIS focal points to use DHIS2 and HeRAMS.

WHO describes the Ministry of Health's Health Information Centre as the body giving technical support to the DHIS2 platform, and sent two of its core team to DHIS2 training in New Delhi on 18-23 November 2024; WHO says it led the strengthening of the national health information system in collaboration with the ministry.

WHO states that all 2024 health information system activities followed the 2024-2025 HIS operational plan, whose focus included strengthening the functionality of the DHIS2 platform, and that the findings of a SCORE assessment (data collected November 2024 to January 2025) will inform a revision of the national HIS strategy.

WHO states that the Ministry of Health and WHO developed a five-year digital transformation roadmap, 2025-2030, promoting integrated digital health solutions including electronic health records and hospital management systems on open-source platforms; it describes no such system as in use.

facts.fact: WHO states that in 2023 it and the Ministry of Health rolled out DHIS2 in 40 municipalities, covering 465 primary health care facilities and 51 hospitals (516 facilities), and that with other partners' support this brought DHIS2 to a 100% implementation rate nationwide; the report names only 'hospitals' and 'PHC facilities', not their levels.

WHO states that 655 health staff from public PHC facilities, hospitals and municipal health administration were trained on DHIS2 in 2023 and given laptops, desktops and tablets to enable data entry, and that 34 supervisory site visits guided staff at health facility level.

WHO counts 465 primary health care facilities among the 516 facilities in 40 municipalities where DHIS2 was rolled out in 2023; it gives no denominator of primary facilities and no national total, and the count is of facilities where the platform was rolled out, not of facilities shown to be entering reports.

WHO states that its support, with UNICEF, IOM, GIZ, the International Rescue Committee, the International Medical Corps and UNFPA, enabled the nationwide DHIS2 rollout in 2023, including the ICT equipment given to trained staff; the report names no domestic budget for the platform and says WHO is urging the Government to make domestic resources available as donor funding falls.

WHO states that the five-year plan to strengthen Libya's health information system ended in 2022 with its objectives partly met, that the 2023 HIS workplan carried forward the expansion of DHIS2 across the country and the integration of vertical programmes' reporting into it, and that a joint WHO and Ministry of Health operational plan for 2024-2025 was endorsed in November 2023.

WHO reports that DHIS2 reached a 100% implementation rate nationwide during 2023 after rollout in a further 40 municipalities, with about 7 million people living in areas that use it; integration of civil registration and vital statistics reporting into DHIS2 was planned for 2024.

facts.fact: Libya Herald reports that the trial operation of the Unified Electronic Health File System was inaugurated in May 2022 at the Ghout al-Shaal Clinical Centre in Tripoli, with the first phase covering two sites, the Ghout al-Shaal clinic in Tripoli and the al-Kish clinic in Benghazi, where the infrastructure had been completed.

The first phase of the Unified Electronic Health File System was set for two facilities the report calls clinics, Ghout al-Shaal in Tripoli (also called a Clinical Centre) and al-Kish in Benghazi, and was presented as improving primary health care services; the report describes a trial run in May 2022, not routine use.

At the May 2022 trial the system's technical committee showed information being entered directly from patients attending the clinic; the system comprises an electronic health file and an individual electronic health card accessible to treating doctors. The report adds that Libya has no family doctor system holding and sharing patient records, so doctors rely on what patients tell them.

Libya Herald describes the Unified Electronic Health File System as a Ministry of Health project under implementation for more than five years as of May 2022, with the acting Minister of Health attending the trial and asking for technical changes to secure citizens' data; no funding source is given.
